Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 11 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 813 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Draft:

Summer projects exist for a simple reason: a break of ten or twelve weeks can wash away a surprising amount of what students learned during the year. Educators have a name for it, the summer slide, and schools respond by assigning work to keep young minds moving. The harder question is who should decide what that work looks like. I believe summer projects should be student-designed, within a frame the teacher provides. When students choose the question they want to chase, the learning is more likely to survive the break, and it is more likely to be learning at all rather than a pile of busywork.

The strongest argument for student design is motivation. Summer is the one stretch of the year when no bell rings and no teacher stands at the front of the room. Any assignment completed then is completed because the student decided to do it. A teacher-designed packet of forty math problems asks a fifteen-year-old to give up beach days for tasks that feel identical to a Tuesday worksheet, and most students respond the only way they can: they rush through it the night before school starts, or they copy answers from a friend. A project the student invented behaves differently. A boy who loves basketball and decides to study how shooting angles affect accuracy will measure, record, and recalculate without anyone nagging him, because he wants to know the answer. Effort that comes from curiosity lasts longer than effort that comes from a deadline.

Student-designed projects also teach skills that teacher-designed ones cannot. Choosing a topic, deciding what counts as evidence, setting a schedule, and finishing without supervision are the habits of independent adults. A teacher-designed project already contains the hardest part, which is deciding what to do. The student only executes. When a student has to plan the project herself, she practices the full cycle of learning. For example, a girl who is bothered by litter in her neighborhood park might design a project in which she surveys the trash for six weeks, sorts it by type, and writes a proposal to the city for more recycling bins. She uses science, math, writing, and civic reasoning, and she does it in a way no single teacher's worksheet could script. Because she built it, she understands why each step matters.

Critics reasonably worry that students left to design their own work will choose something easy, or nothing at all. A student might propose to "watch documentaries" and call it research. This concern is real, but it is an argument for guidance, not for taking control away. The best arrangement is a partnership. Before school lets out, the teacher sets requirements: the project must involve a question, a method, a record of progress, and a final product shared in the fall. Students then submit a short proposal, and the teacher approves it or sends it back for revision. This keeps rigor in place while leaving the choice of subject with the student. A teacher can tell a vague idea from a workable one, and a quick conversation in June can turn "watch documentaries" into "compare how three documentaries portray the same historical event and write a review of which is most accurate."

Another objection is fairness. Some students come from homes with books, computers, and parents who help, while others do not. A teacher-designed project at least gives everyone the same task. Yet equal tasks do not produce equal results, since the student with resources still finishes faster and better. Student design can actually narrow the gap, because a child can build a project from what is available to her. A student without internet access can interview her grandmother about family history, write a short biography, and draw a map of where the family has lived. That project needs a notebook and a conversation, not a subscription. Teachers can further level the field by offering a list of free options and by allowing the fall presentation to take many forms, such as an essay, a model, a video, or a talk.

Finally, student-designed projects make the first week back in September better for everyone. Instead of collecting identical packets that all look the same, a teacher receives a room full of different discoveries. Students have something real to share, and classmates learn from each other. Listening to a peer explain what she found about the park litter is far more engaging than reading a stack of answers to the same twenty questions.

Summer should keep students learning, but it should also let them enjoy learning. Teachers know what a good project requires, and students know what interests them. By having teachers set the standards and students set the topics, schools can get both rigor and enthusiasm. That combination is what turns a required assignment into the kind of work students might do even if no one asked them to.
